why: Both wrap the same single call site identically, but B found the gap that decides whether the migration is real in production — the Dockerfile copied only llmcord.py, so a built image would silently fall back to the no-op wrapper and route nothing — and then went deeper on the system: nine measured, validated branches covering the model/effort decision (with a conservative alternative marked mutually exclusive), the cacheable prefix, the Router policy, silent failures, the multiplicative prompt budget, per-message client construction, and catalog-driven vision. A's ranking is sound and its caching and Flex measurements are excellent, but four of its seven improvements are unbuilt proposals and its headline claim that routing alone halves the bill leans on Flex being the account default rather than on anything the migration changed.
A_best: The cacheable-prefix item: it identified the per-second clock at the head of every prompt as the app's most expensive request-shape defect and proved it on a realistic 2,530-token chain with cached_tokens, including the finding that a stable prefix does the work without prompt_cache_key.
B_best: Catching that the Dockerfile's `COPY llmcord.py` would leave the documented docker deployment silently unrouted — because the guarded import fails open with nothing in the logs — which is the difference between a migration that ships and one that only works in the dev checkout.
A_worst: Framing the move itself as '-48% per reply' when Flex is already the account default, and leaving the fallback list, output cap, catalog capabilities and provider consolidation as proposals, so the Router-only leverage it ranks highest is mostly unbuilt.
B_worst: Merging a fallbacks list on every request while acknowledging the least-capable candidate caps context, tools and modalities — a standing behaviour risk on a bot that replays 25 messages — and a sprawling 14-item report whose Switchyard branch is never explained.
